Introduction to Oscilloscopes

Alright, let’s get started. Today we’re going to be learning something that may sound a little fancy, but it actually is not. We’ll be learning a little bit about oscilloscopes first, and then what’s called a Fourier transform.

Has anybody heard of or maybe worked with an oscilloscope before? No? What’s an oscilloscope? Is that the thing that a doctor has? You know, they put it on your chest and listen to your heartbeat. No, that’s a stethoscope. An oscilloscope is really any kind of instrument that will measure your signal as a function of time. So, like the monitor that’s next to a patient in a hospital measuring a heartbeat, that’s sort of a type of oscilloscope as well. The one that goes beep, beep, beep, beep.

Instead of measuring a patient’s heartbeat, we’re going to look at a simple sinusoidal wave. We’ve seen it over and over. This looks to be an undamped sine wave. There’s really no indication of the amplitude of the displacement getting smaller with time; it seems to be staying constant.

Let’s look at a quick example to get you back into the swing of things.

The question asks: if the oscilloscope’s time base is set to 1\text{ ms} per division, what is the frequency of the wave shown in the image?

What on earth does that mean? Remember, the horizontal axis here is time, denoted by t. The vertical axis here is the signal, typically measured in volts (V). The signal is just going up and down in a sinusoidal fashion.

"One millisecond per division" just means that each box you see on the horizontal grid is 1\text{ ms} wide. Later on, you’ll see expressions like 1\text{ V} per division or 5\text{ V} per division. That refers to the vertical axis, because typically the signal is measuring electrical voltage.

So, what is the frequency of the wave? To find the frequency, I might ask myself: what is the period? The period, denoted by T, is just the time it takes for one complete cycle of the wave. If I start at a peak and end at the next peak, I will have gone through one full cycle.

Looking at the grid, one full cycle spans two of those divisions. Since each division is 1\text{ ms}, the period is: \begin{equation} T = 2\text{ ms} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s} \tag{1} \end{equation}

Frequency, denoted by f, is the inverse of the period: \begin{equation} f = \frac{1}{T} \tag{2} \end{equation}

Plugging in our period: \begin{align} f &= \frac{1}{2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}} \tag{3}\\ &= \frac{1}{2} \times 10^3\text{ s}^{-1} \tag{4}\\ &= 500\text{ s}^{-1} \tag{5}\\ &= 500\text{ Hz} \tag{6} \end{align}

So, we’re seeing a sine signal with a frequency of 500\text{ Hz}. This means it takes 2\text{ ms} for one complete cycle, and the wave undergoes 500 cycles every second.

Let’s try another one.

Now the time base is set to 5\text{ ms} per division. What is the frequency?

The period is still two divisions, but now each division is 5\text{ ms}. So the period is: \begin{equation} T = 2 \times 5\text{ ms} = 10\text{ ms} = 10 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s} = 0.01\text{ s} \tag{7} \end{equation}

The frequency is: \begin{equation} f = \frac{1}{0.01\text{ s}} = 100\text{ Hz} \tag{8} \end{equation}

The Sound of Music: Harmonics and Overtones

Now, does anybody feel like they want to play with an oscilloscope right now? We don’t have a real oscilloscope, but we can use a virtual one on your laptop or phone.

If you search for "virtual oscilloscope" (like the one from academo.org), you can pick up sound directly from your microphone.

I warned you there might be some singing involved today! I’d like to hear some musical notes coming from all your mouths.

Some of you have probably listened to a symphonic orchestra tuning before a performance. They’re all trying to calibrate their notes so they’re in sync, usually tuning to the note A.

This A note presumably has a frequency of 440\text{ Hz}. Naively, you might think that if you feed this orchestra tuning into the oscilloscope, you would just see a pure sinusoidal wave with a frequency of 440\text{ Hz}.

What is the period of a 440\text{ Hz} wave? \begin{equation} T = \frac{1}{440\text{ Hz}} \approx 2.27\text{ ms} \tag{9} \end{equation}

But if you actually look at the signal from an instrument (or your voice) singing an A, does it look like a pure sine wave?

No, it looks a little jagged. Why is that? Is it because our voices suck? No, all your voices are beautiful!

The reason is that no instruments, even though they play the same note, produce a pure sine wave. How come the note A played by a piano sounds different from the same note played by a trumpet? They have the same fundamental frequency, but they sound different because of resonance and what are called overtones or harmonics.

In addition to the fundamental frequency, you have a mix of higher frequencies.

Let’s say our fundamental frequency is f_1 = 440\text{ Hz}. The angular frequency is \omega_1 = 2\pi f_1.

Mixed in with that, you can have a signal with twice the frequency: 2\omega_1. This is called the first overtone or the second harmonic. You can also have the third harmonic (3\omega_1), the fourth harmonic (4\omega_1), and so on.

The way these harmonics are combined—their relative amplitudes—determines the unique sound or "timbre" of the instrument or voice. You can have an infinite number of combinations.

Fourier Series

This is the fundamental idea behind what’s called a Fourier series (or Fourier sine series).

We can represent a complex periodic signal f(t) as a sum of sine waves: \begin{align} f(t) &= A_1 \sin(\omega_1 t) \nonumber \\ &\quad + A_2 \sin(2\omega_1 t) \nonumber \\ &\quad + A_3 \sin(3\omega_1 t) \nonumber \\ &\quad + A_4 \sin(4\omega_1 t) \nonumber \\ &\quad + \dots \tag{10} \end{align}

Here, \omega_1 is the fundamental angular frequency, and the coefficients A_n represent the amplitude of each harmonic.

We can write this more compactly using summation notation: \begin{equation} f(t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n \sin(n \omega_1 t) \tag{11} \end{equation}

In practice, we don’t go to infinity; we cut it off at some point.

Fourier Transform in Action

Let’s look at some actual data. I recorded myself singing a "high A" and a "low A" and ran it through a Python script to perform a Fourier transform.

A Fourier transform takes a signal in the time domain (like our jagged oscilloscope trace) and converts it into the frequency domain. It tells you exactly how much of each harmonic (A_n) is present in the signal.

Let’s look at the high A first. My voice is a little lower, so my fundamental frequency for this note was around 220\text{ Hz}.

The top plot is the raw voice print—the signal versus time. The bottom plot is the Fourier spectrum. You can clearly see a massive peak at the fundamental frequency of 220\text{ Hz} (the 1st harmonic). But you also see peaks at 440\text{ Hz} (the 2nd harmonic) and 660\text{ Hz} (the 3rd harmonic). This spectrum describes the unique nature of my voice singing that note.

Now, what if I sing a low A, exactly one octave lower? An octave lower means the frequency is halved. So we expect the fundamental frequency to be around 110\text{ Hz}.

In the real-time data (top), the oscillations are sparser—about two times sparser than before, as expected. In the frequency spectrum (bottom), we see a peak around 110\text{ Hz}. We also see the second harmonic at 220\text{ Hz}, the third at 330\text{ Hz}, and the fourth at 440\text{ Hz}.

This is the basic idea behind a Fourier transform. You feed in some periodic data that might look complicated, and the computer tells you how much of each harmonic is present. This is widely used in audio analysis, but also in other areas of science, like FTIR (Fourier Transform Infrared) spectroscopy, to boost signal clarity.
